Fairly typical solitaire game, similar to others by this developer.

The Voice acting is good.
The story is a typical one for games like this, not bad, but not deep. 
(If you are expecting a seriously deep and compelling story- play an RPG, not a solitaire game.).
The story is delivered via the opening scene when you first launch the game, and then when you complete a chapter you get a new page with more story. 
It's okay- medieval dragon-slaying fantasy type stuff, probably fine for younger kids with parental supervision. Nothing too gory or scary, though the sudden appearance of the fire-breather while playing a table might be a bit if a scare for really young kids.
Typical grind grind grind to complete objectives.
Expect to replay some hands several times if you are going for all three-stars on every level.
You can replay tables 1-9 as many times as you like to perfect them alll, but the last able (10) cannot be replayed without replaying the entire chapter.

[b][u]***Accessibility***[/u][/b]
The game can be played with a mouse only, one-handed.

Everything delivered via voice acting is also delivered via text- there are no text scaling options, but the text does not disappear or move too fast to read. You must click to progress past, so you have all the time you need. Should be very playable for Deaf and HoH players. Some text is smallish- may be tougher for players with low vision, even in full-screen.

No colorblindness settings- the map is marked with red dots (completed chapters) and larger green dots (the chapter you are playing). The size difference between the two should help, but you may need to use machine settings to adjust colors, depending on what form of color-blindness you have.

The UI and things like navigation to the store are not great- you have to click "Menu" while you are at the table, then choose "Map" then "Store", to be able to buy buffs and potions.  Wild cards are bought while playing a table, using a [+] in the lower right side of the screen.
It isn't well explained, even with the tutorial turned on. Can be a bit illogical feeling and a bit confusing.

3 different difficulty modes, with no achievements tied to difficulty. So that's a nice thing for people who want or need an easier mode, and for those who really like to challenge themselves.
***************************************************************

Again, it's a fairly typical solitaire/story game, heavy grind with a reasonably good story for this type of game.
100% Achievements should be possible for pretty much anyone, but it won't be quick.

Recommended, especially on sale. The game has faults, but runs well even on a toaster, and no bugs encountered by me at the time of this review. Good time killer, suitable for short sessions (each table only lasts for 5-15 minutes depending on whether you replay it), or longer sessions if you like. Just don't expect anything out-of-the-ordinary or fresh. But worth a buy, even so.

I played this not long after completing [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/tablis/recommended/432190/]Chef Solitaire: USA[/url] so it's natural I'll compare the two. Besides, it's the same company. Curse of the Dragons is superior in [i]almost[/i] every respect: graphics, story, voice acting. The powerups and items are about similarily entertaining. But there is one big downside I need to talk about. In Chef Solitaire every hand is... self-contained, for lack of a better word. What I mean by that, is that it has its own goals and if you fail those, you just retry that one hand. Here, goals are assigned per level, and one level is ten hands. If you fail even one of the goals, you have to redo all ten hands. That feels like terrible design. It caused [i]a situation[/i] where I modified my gold gain for a level because I saw I was going to fail it and did not want to waste time redoing it. Hacking a solitaire game is a low I'd never imagine myself stooping to, but here we are. I seriously considered giving a thumbs downs but because this happened only once, it's acceptable. The objectives are actually well balanced to create tension but when all tools are used, it's not a big deal. And besides, I didn't feel like it's a chore to finish, unlike the other game.

I received Legends of Solitaire: Curse of the Dragons in a Revills two-pack. This is easily their worst solitaire game - however, it was also their first. I've also played Chef Solitaire and Home Run Solitaire, and the developer has gotten better with each outing. Although this one has a mildly amusing fantasy aesthetic, complete with the narration of what sounds like a wizened old man, there just isn't much here to set it apart. 

You gain a couple of abilities as you play, and you'll have four to choose from at the end of the game. One (the wizard) removes a random card from the board, which can actually be a card that is face down underneath another. Therefore, there are many times that this ability is completely useless in helping you clear the board. Another ability (the dwarf) allows you to randomly flip over a face-down card. This one is so useless that I barely used it during the entire game, regardless of whether it was available. The third ability (the goblin) throws down a card that you can use to remove another from the board, so finally our abilities are getting useful. The last (the elf) allows you to pull a card down from the board to serve as your active card. This ability is the most useful one, and can allow you to create and maintain long combos.

I remember there being another ability as well, but it actually is replaced later in the game. Unfortunately, you can't choose which ability is replaced - I would've loved to get rid of the dwarf.

Outside of the mostly bland abilities, there are also a few absurdly challenging stages at the end. Even after playing quite a few of these solitaire titles, I failed the 38th stage perhaps five times in a row. Considering that each stage consists of ten levels, this was quite a time-consuming endeavor. Eventually, I found that you could sort of "quit" a stage on the last level, and re-enter from the map at level one. For some reason, when you do this the game maintains the progress you had made thus far. Therefore, in essence, you might have 18 levels (or perhaps as many as you want) to earn the amount of gold or "perfects" the game requires for progression.

Legends of Solitaire: Curse of the Dragons is fine, I suppose, even if a little boring. However, I can't recommend it when there are much more engaging solitaire titles (even by the same developer) on the Steam store.

Il gioco è molto carino, il tipico solitario in cui bisogna ripulire il campo di gioco selezionando le carte che sono di una unità superiore o inferiore al valore della carta del giocatore.
Il fulcro del gioco è la modalità storia, che consta di 400 schemi di gioco. Alla base vi è il racconto di un gruppo di eroi che deve liberare il regno dall'oppressione dei draghi. Nulla di che, solo un pretesto che pian piano si svolge lungo 40 capitoli, ognuno costituito da 10 "tavoli" (quindi 400 in tutto), ma raccontato con una bella voce e con una certa classe.
All'inizio di ogni capitolo vengono posti degli obiettivi (ad esempio, fare una combo di almeno tot mosse, o ripulire completamente il campo di gioco per un certo numero di volte). Per raggiungere gli obiettivi, man mano che il gioco va avanti si aggiungono al party dei personaggi che hanno mosse speciali (ad esempio eliminare una carta dal terreno di gioco), oppure si accumula denaro che serve ad acquistare oggetti che permettono di facilitare la vita al giocatore (chiavi per aprire lucchetti che bloccano certe carte, spade e armi per distruggere ostacoli ecc...).
400 livelli sono tanti e in circa 14/15 ore il gioco impegna piacevolmente, sebbene alla fin fine non si dimostri mai difficile, nemmeno nei quadri avanzati (anche grazie ai poteri bonus).
Vi sono anche altre due modalità di gioco libero, ma sono inutili e poco divertenti.
Menzione d'onore per le canzoncine in sottofondo, piuttosto varie e fischiettabili, nonchè adatte al contesto, ovvero rilassanti.
Da consigliare anche a chi cerca di fare achievement facili: finirete il gioco portandoli a termine tutti.

We're all pretty familiar with the way that solitaire works.  The rules for this one -- you have to choose cards that are sequential, not necessarily alternating between red and black suits.  The sequence can move up or down -- for example, when you have a "four" exposed you can either play a three or a five on it.

You get bonus points for the number of cards you can play in sequence.  You also achieve bonus points for various combinations and permutations.

For me -- there are so many free versions of solitaire out there that this one isn't necessary.  Yes, there is an overarching plot -- you are a group of fantasy adventurers journeying through the dangerous countryside, fighting orcs and dragons as you go.  But truly the requirements from advancing one level to another are pretty arbitrary.  And anyone who plays solitaire knows that your ultimate success is largely based on luck.

Games based on luck, for me, begin to feel tedious.  Grinding is an unpleasant label you might apply to it.  Listen, I've had my fill of grinding after playing WoW for seven years.  The title "The Insane" was enough to convience me that I was wasting my life on sh*t that didn't matter.

So I get pissed off at games that essentially become grinding episodes.  The graphics are cool, the sound is passable, and the game enjoyable enough.  It's just that I think that there are plenty of free versions out there that makes me conclude that this one isn't worth spending money on.

As always, readers should view what I write seen through the lens of the casual gamer -- that is, someone who has limited time due to family, a career, and soul-crushing student loan debt.

Save yourself $9.  Buy your kids some cookies at Target.

Great game! You'll play at least 400 hands... 40 levels of 10 hands each... with each level having several objectives that must be satisfied in order to unlock the next level. You'll have to replay the level, not just one hand but ten, if you don't satisfy the level's objectives. The objectives do get somewhat more difficult at the higher levels, so you might want to play on "easy" the first time.

A different kind of pace; a solitaire variant with a smattering of extracurricular mechanisms at work. Could use more depth in those mechanisms, some rpg progression, and more actual game types of solitaire, but overall still a good game. One hopes to see further entries in the series that are similarly fantastically themed, exploring this sort of creative casual adventure (!) design.
